exam: A 2‑year‑old boy presents with a febrile UTI. What is the first investigation you would order? — Urine culture to confirm infection and guide antibiotics.
A child with grade III VUR is on prophylaxis but develops a second febrile UTI. What is the next step? — Re‑evaluate with VCUG; consider surgical correction if infection persists.
Why is a VCUG preferred over ultrasound for diagnosing VUR? — VCUG visualises the direction and grade of reflux; ultrasound only shows hydronephrosis.
A patient with VUR develops hypertension. What is the likely mechanism? — Renal scarring reduces nephron number, activating the renin‑angiotensin system.
Which antibiotic is avoided in VUR patients with penicillin allergy? — Fluoroquinolones are avoided due to risk of cartilage damage in children.
A low‑resource hospital cannot perform VCUG. What alternative imaging can you use? — Renal ultrasound to look for hydronephrosis and DMSA scan if available for scarring.
ai.title: Vesicoureteral Reflux in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A congenital or acquired back‑flow of urine from bladder to kidney that predisposes to infection and scarring. Diagnosis relies on imaging, and treatment balances infection control with surgical correction.

b: Congenital defect of the ureterovesical junction (UVJ)
Secondary causes: bladder outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder, post‑renal infection
sections.p: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and kidney. It is most often congenital, but can be secondary to bladder outlet obstruction or infection.

t.b: Shows the direction and grade of reflux; the gold standard for diagnosis. A positive study confirms VUR.

b: Grade I–II: reflux to pelvis, minimal damage
Grade III–IV: reflux to calyces, moderate scarring
Grade V: reflux to renal parenchyma, severe scarring
sections.p: VUR is graded I–V based on the extent of reflux and renal damage. Higher grades carry greater risk of scarring and hypertension.
